elements.content: Grammar focus: Distancing Passive Reporting.

Use the impersonal form when the claim itself is the topic: It is alleged that funds were moved. Use the personal form when the person is the topic and the claim is background: He is alleged to have moved the funds. The reporting verb decides the strength: alleged signals dispute, understood signals a briefing, reported signals the press.

It is said that + clause — impersonal report: it is said that the plan failed
X is said to + infinitive — report about a present state: the plan is said to be unworkable
X is said to have + participle — report about the past: the plan is said to have failed
It is alleged / reported / understood — claim without commitment: it is alleged that funds were moved
X is believed / thought / expected to — belief or expectation: the talks are expected to resume
X is understood to — quiet official confirmation: the board is understood to have voted
Guided practice: choose the correct option.
1. Complete: 'The minister ___ to have known about the payment.'
2. Which reporting verb signals a briefing rather than a rumour?
3. Complete: 'It ___ that the talks collapsed.'
Read and listen: three examples in context.

It is reported that the talks collapsed. — The talks are reported to have collapsed. (Source removed, claim kept.)
It is believed that she resigned. — She is believed to have resigned. (Perfect infinitive for a past event.)
Officials think the delay will grow. — The delay is expected to grow. (Expectation reported, not predicted.)
What do you observe?

Two shapes carry the same claim. The impersonal shape opens with it is plus a reporting verb and a that-clause: it is said that he left. The personal shape moves the subject forward and uses the infinitive: he is said to have left. For a past event the infinitive is perfect (to have left); for a simultaneous state it is simple (he is said to be abroad).
1. Which shape needs a perfect infinitive?
options: A claim about a past event.
A claim about a present state.

elements.content: 2. What does the passive do to the source?
options: It removes the source from the sentence.
It names the source at the end.

elements.content: State the rule in one sentence, without looking at the table.
Freer production: I can report what people are said to think, do or have done.

Success criteria:
- I can report a claim without naming the source.
- I can choose between it is said that and X is said to.
- I can use a perfect infinitive for a past claim.
Role play: put your position in ninety seconds; your partner notes every use of the target structure.
Frequent errors and correction:

❌ It is said that he left yesterday, he is said to leave yesterday (present infinitive for a past event) → ✅ He is said to have left yesterday
❌ It is believed that she is resigning, she is believed resigning (no infinitive after the reporting verb) → ✅ She is believed to be resigning
Correct these sentences: say what is wrong, then give the right version.
Acceptable variants:

It is understood that the deal was signed in June.
The deal is understood to have been signed in June.
The results are expected to be published on Friday.
Adapt the same task to the group:

- Individual: five sentences with the structure, on the topic of the lesson.
- Pair: a ten-line dialogue where distancing passive reporting carries the argument.
- Group: a six-minute debate, two sides, the structure required in every turn.
- Professional audience: transpose the structure into a memo.
- Academic audience: transpose it into a paragraph of analysis.
